passage:
Rafiq twisted the tiffin lid off. "Watch, Uma. Twist and pop."
"Twist!" Uma grabbed the raisin box and turned it hard. The lid stayed shut.
"Abbu did. Twist," Uma said, and turned it again, the same way.
"Almost, jaan. Look at my hand. Other way."
Uma frowned at the box, then at Rafiq's fingers.
"Want to see it slowly?"
"Again!" Uma said.

qa.q: What did Uma try to open?
qa.a: Uma tried to open the raisin box.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when the lid stayed shut?
qa.a: Uma was puzzled but determined, shown by the frown, the second twist and the shout of "Again!"

qa.q: What could Uma do differently to get the lid off, and why?
qa.a: Uma could turn the lid the other way, watching Rafiq's hand, because copying the motion only works if the direction matches too.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Uma's copying?
qa.a: Rafiq sees his child copying him closely and probably feels amused and proud, which is why he offers to show it slowly.

grounding: A toddler copies the twisting wrist motion of the father but turns the lid the wrong way.

passage:
Note for Nilesh's parents, Tuesday
At drop-off today Nilesh watched his papa, Anand, unscrew the steel tiffin to show me his lunch. At snack time he picked up the small box of raisins and turned his wrist exactly the way Papa had. He turned it the wrong way, so the lid only tightened. He frowned and tried again, same way. I opened my own box slowly beside him so he could see the direction.

qa.q: What did Nilesh pick up at snack time?
qa.a: He picked up the small box of raisins.

qa.q: What was Nilesh thinking when he turned his wrist like Papa?
qa.a: He seemed hopeful and sure that copying Papa's twist would open any box, then puzzled when the lid only tightened.

qa.q: What did the note-writer try, and why might it help?
qa.a: They opened their own box slowly beside him, so he could see which way to turn instead of being told.

qa.q: How might Anand feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel touched that Nilesh copies him closely, and interested that the copy did not quite fit.

grounding: A caregiver's note describes a toddler copying his father's twisting motion on a raisin box but twisting the wrong way.

passage: Before going to the paddy, Bidisha's baba, Vaibhav, twisted open his steel tiffin on the verandah and ate a quick bite of rice. Bidisha watched from her mat. After he left, she crawled to the plastic jar of raisins by the grinding stone, gripped the lid and twisted her wrist hard, just like him. The lid didn't move. She twisted again, the same way, tongue poking out, then banged the jar down and stared at it.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav eat on the verandah?
qa.a: He ate a quick bite of rice.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's stare at the jar suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems puzzled and a bit frustrated that the twist that worked for Baba does nothing for her.

qa.q: What else could help Bidisha open the jar?
qa.a: Showing her the twist slowly the other way, or letting her ask a grown-up, because her copy has the motion but not the direction.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see this if he had stayed to watch?
qa.a: He would probably feel proud and amused that she copied him, and might show her which way to turn.

grounding: A toddler copies her father's twisting of a tiffin on a raisin jar, but the twist goes the wrong way and it stays shut.
